newsitem.title: ITALY: Corruption probe shakes summer lull in Rome.
newsitem.headline: Corruption probe shakes summer lull in Rome.

text.p: A corruption probe into alleged links between the Rome judiciary and building firms has shattered Italy's summer calm, sending politicians, magistrates and tycoons rushing from the beaches to their lawyers' offices.
Newspapers reported on Wednesday that more than 30 people are under official investigation in the case, which is being spearheaded by magistrates in the central city of Perugia.
A further 70 are expected to give evidence before the end of the month in an investigation which has re-ignited interest in Italy's faltering campaign to root out high-level corruption.

The probes have already forced the head of the anti-Mafia police to resign while Minister for Foreign Trade Augusto Fantozzi was forced to break off his holiday last week to explain his links with a leading suspect in the inquiries.
The case revolves around one of Rome's top tax experts, Sergio Melpignano, and building magnate Domenico Bonifaci.

Both men are being held in prison while magistrates look into charges that they controlled huge slush funds to corrupt Rome judges in cases such as the infamous Enimont scandal, a major milestone in the mass graft probes of the early 1990s.
A Perugia court on Wednesday rejected a defence bid to have Bonifaci and Melpignano released from jail.
"Not only does there remain serious evidence of guilt, as seen in the custody order, but this evidence has been hardened by subsequent investigations," the court ruling said.

Unlike in previous probes headed by the elite anti-graft team of "Clean Hands" prosecutors in Milan, Perugia magistrates have kept largely tight-lipped about their inquiries and few details have emerged in Italy's normally well-informed press.
But newspapers agree that the case has sucked in a host of well-known figures from the Rome establishment.

"At the centre of the investigations are (Rome's) most important construction chiefs," the daily Corriere della Sera said on Wednesday. "The probe will cause perhaps 100 people to miss their end-of August holidays," it added.

Fantozzi was so worried by the implications of the case that, when old photographs were published last week of him leaving a cafe with Melpignano, he ended his summer break and rushed to Perugia to explain what he had been doing.
The minister, who is not under investigation in the case, said he had merely sought to use Melpignano's influence to get a Rome newspaper to stop printing unfavourable articles about him.
This admission drew mutterings of disapproval from some government allies but Prime Minister Romano Prodi rallied to his defence and said it was not a matter for him to resign over.
Perugia magistrates believe Melpignano and Bonifaci controlled numerous slush funds, including some 39 billion lire ($21.6 million) earmarked for bribes in the Enimont case.
The Enimont scandal was the single most important case to emerge from the vast "Clean Hands" graft investigations that broke in 1992 and toppled Italy's corrupt political old guard.
It involved the chemical company Montedison, which paid more than $100 million in kickbacks to extricate itself from a disastrous joint venture with state energy company ENI. ($1 = 1,805 lire)
